title: Wealth Inequality and Planetary Boundaries in a Stylized Agent-Based Model
authors: Thomas Valade, Michael Benzaquen, Matthieu Cristelli, Stanislao Gualdi, Pierre Lenders
abstract: At the intersection of rising wealth inequality and intensifying environmental pressures, we investigate a reverse causal relationship that has received comparatively little attention: wealth inequality may not only be a consequence of environmental crises, but also act as a structural obstacle to the ecological transition itself. We develop a stylized agent-based model in which heterogeneous agents, whose initial wealth follows a Pareto distribution, allocate their income between either a Brown or a Green sector through a utility function. The function is designed to capture the trade-off between short-term returns and exposure to long-term systemic risks. A central ingredient is that wealthier agents perceive themselves as less vulnerable to environmental shocks, thereby reducing the amount of resources available for the transition. We show that, beyond inequality thresholds compatible with those observed in most developed countries, the economy remains locked in a Brown regime, even when a substantial share of agents is sensitive to externalities. We then assess a set of stylized fiscal policies (basic income, carbon taxation, Green incentives, and a combined scheme) and find that their effectiveness depends strongly on the inequality regime and on the regressivity embedded in the fiscal mechanism, revealing multidimensional trade-offs between transition speed, cumulative environmental destruction, growth, and fiscal pressure.
summary: This work uses an Agent-Based Model to explore how wealth inequality impedes the transition to a sustainable 'Green' economy. It finds that high levels of inequality can lock economies into polluting regimes, even when environmental risks are known. The results highlight that no single policy is universally optimal; effective intervention requires tailoring mechanisms (taxation vs. incentives) to the specific level of existing economic disparity.
main_problem: The study investigates whether wealth inequality acts as a structural obstacle preventing an economy from undergoing an ecological transition toward sustainability, rather than merely being a consequence of environmental damage.
main_result: The research demonstrates that beyond certain thresholds of wealth inequality, the economy can become locked in a high-emission 'Brown' regime, regardless of agent sensitivity to climate externalities. The effectiveness of policy interventions depends critically on the existing level of inequality and the regressivity embedded in the fiscal mechanism.
method: The authors employ a stylized Agent-Based Model (ABM) simulating heterogeneous agents allocating income between environmentally damaging ('Brown') and sustainable ('Green') sectors based on utility maximization.
model_or_system: The model features agents with initial wealth following a Pareto distribution, making decentralized investment decisions influenced by short-term returns versus long-term systemic environmental risks. The dynamics are governed by equations describing income rates and agent utility differences related to externalities.
key_observables: Gini coefficient, Time to Transition ($T_{2T}$), cumulative environmental destruction ($\langle\omega_{	ext{loss}}(t)angle$), aggregate Green/Brown wealth shares, and policy performance metrics (e.g., reduction in $T_{2T}$).
important_parameters: Initial wealth heterogeneity ($	ext{Gini}_0$), externality awareness weight ($\lambda$), time scales for tech inertia ($	au$) and external impact decay ($	heta$), and parameters defining fiscal mechanisms.
main_assumptions: Agents are assumed to be rational utility maximizers; the model is stylized, representing an exploratory framework rather than a precise forecast of reality. A key assumption is that wealthier agents discount long-term environmental risks more heavily.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phase diagrams showing transition possibility thresholds based on inequality, and radar plots comparing the multidimensional performance trade-offs (e.g., speed vs. cost) across various policy combinations.
paper_structure: The paper develops an ABM framework to model wealth allocation between two sectors; it establishes that high initial inequality can trap the system in a poor state; subsequently, it compares multiple fiscal policies (BI, carbon tax, incentives) by analyzing their impact on transition speed and environmental outcomes across different inequality regimes.
why_interesting: While not directly quantum mechanical, the use of complex non-equilibrium dynamics, phase transitions (Brown to Green regime), and agent heterogeneity mirrors concepts found in statistical physics models of critical phenomena or pattern formation far from equilibrium.
